newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open up, sales data seen friendly.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open up, sales data seen friendly.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened higher on Tuesday ahead of a weekly report on early September stores sales that is expected to be market-friendly.
"We get a lot of little data today," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A. "It will be interesting to see how the store selling period began in September."
Stiles said that after a strong Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi report on retail sales for the last week of August, "you can't expect much" of a gain in the first week of September.
"We expect the (Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi) report to be a bit friendly and slightly supportive for the market," said James Blumenthal, economist at MCM Moneywatch.
Stiles said there are "plenty of people worried about consumers spending at a healthy pace."
Stiles said the Redbook report on chain and department store sales due in the afternoon "is expected to start out positive" in terms of early September sales activity.
Tuesday's trading session will be punctuated by a handful of second-tier data, analysts said.

Besides the privately culled reports on store sales in the first week of September, the market gets four different reports at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT -- July wholesale inventories, revised second-quarter productivity, second-quarter current account and the August business survey from the Richmond Federal Reserve.
July wholesales inventories are expected to be up 0.3 percent, according to economists polled by Reuters, versus unchanged level in June.
But Stiles said that report was unlikely to influence the market. "People are more interested in September data than in what happened in July," he said.
Revised second-quarter non-farm productivity is expected to be up 0.4 percent from down 0.1 percent in the first quarter.
"That means unit labor costs should be revised down a touch," said Stiles.
The second quarter current account deficit is expected to be $34.8 billion, little changed from the $35.59 billion deficit that prevailed in the first quarter.
In July the manufacturing shipments index of the Richmond Fed's business survey was down seven while the services index gave a reading of 24.
The dollar opened higher as the tone for the U.S. unit remained bullish due to interest-rate differentials.
Stiles called the dollar "very strong" and said it bore watching as a potential factor in the bond market's performance.
But allowing for the heavy does of secondary data due today, analysts said the market was still more interested in data to come later in the week.

The Fed's Beige Book, an anecdotal description of business conditions around the nation, is due on Wednesday. And the market gets the August Producer Price Index (PPI) on Thursday and August Consumer Price Index (CPI) and retail sales reports on Friday.
"The retail sales report is important but not as important as the PPI and CPI as far as (shaping) the market's view of Fed policy," said Blumenthal.
With significant data in the offing, analysts said they did not expect the market to break into any fresh territory today.
"Basically it's a matter of drifting in range trading ahead of the data," said Blumenthal.
In early trade, the 6-3/4 percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond was up 4/32 to 96-4/32, yielding 7.06 percent.

At the short end of the maturity range, three- and six-month Treasury bill rates were each down one basis point to 5.13 percent and 5.29 percent, respectively. The one-year bill rate was down one basis point to 5.54 percent.

The two-year note was up 1/32 to 99-23/32, yielding 6.28 percent. The five-year note was up 1/32 to 99-12/32, yielding 6.65 percent, and the 10-year note was up 1/32 to 100-27/32, yielding 6.88 percent.
